newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway, Swedish firms suprised by funds scandal.
newsitem.headline: Norway, Swedish firms suprised by funds scandal.

text.p: Two small Norwegian and Swedish firms said they were surprised on Friday to learn their main shareholder is investment fund group Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM), currently embroiled in a financial scandal.
Norwegian software house Sysdeco Group ASA and Swedish engineering company Sintercast AB both said they were unaware of the heavy interest shown in them by the British group.

MGAM on Monday suspended dealing in three funds -- MG European Growth Trust, MG Europa and Dublin-listed MG European Capital Growth -- and launched an investigation into possible irregularities on certain unquoted securities.
Trading in the funds was resumed three days later after MGAM suspended two fund managers, Peter Young and Stewart Armer.
MGAM said that during the enquiries it had discovered that it could own up to 57 percent of the A shares in Sintercast and up to 98 percent of the group's B shares.

"It was a surprise to us that Morgan Grenfell may own as much as 57 percent of Sintercast," the company's Chairman Bo Ramfors told Reuters. "We knew they had a large stake but we were unaware that it could be a majority holding."
Sintercast's share price has fallen more than 30 percent this week to 255 Swedish crowns at the close on Friday from 374 crowns on Monday.
MGAM's parent company Deutsche Bank confirmed a previous MGAM statement that the group may hold 51 percent in Sysdeco.
Under Norwegian securities regulations, a company is obliged to make an offer to the remaining shareholders once it has acquired 45 percent or more of the issued equity in a concern.
Bourse authorities on Thursday transferred Sysdeco to a watch list pending further information of the fund's intentions.

Deutsche Bank explained the acquisition in Sysdeco "had not received appropriate internal authorisations". It said neither did it intend to buy out the remaining stock, nor did it expect to be required by law to make an offer.

"I'm sure this will be sorted out quickly," said Sysdeco President Tor Alfheim. "We have no reason to be concerned, the funding behind the group, Deutsche Bank, is impeccable. But we would prefer to have a wider spread of shareholders."

MGAM funds holds an interest in another Oslo-listed company, high-technology group Nera ASA Nera President Asbjoern Birkeland said he was aware of MGAM's dealings in the group but he was not concerned at this week's events.

In a separate thread to the tangled web, the Norwegian Banking, Securities and Insurance Commission launched an investigation into Oslo-based brokerage house FIBA Nordic Securities AS over its cooperation with a London-based FIBA-linked broker which had dealings with MGAM.

A commission official said it had written to FIBA asking for a full report on its role performing back office functions for FIBA Nordic Securities (UK) Ltd, also known as FIBA Nordic Securities (FNS). FNS sold unlisted securities to, and valued securities for the three MGAM funds under investigation.

"The commission, as a result of this, wants a full report on the cooperation between the Norwegian and the English FIBA, including how the tasks were carried out legally and how they were done in practise," the commission's letter said.
Swedish financial market regulation body Finansinspektionen said it was keeping a watch over the funds' case.
